narrativeProgression.description: Salivary glands and lymph nodes are identified.
The heart, aorta, and carotid arteries are shown.
The diaphragm and liver are discussed.
The absence of a gallbladder is noted, and the stomach is identified.
The spleen and pancreas are shown.
The duodenum, jejunum, cecum, and ileum are traced.
The ascending, transverse, and descending colon are identified, leading to the rectum.
The uterine horns and ovaries are briefly mentioned.
The urinary bladder, ureters, and kidneys are shown.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: We have a dissected rat. I'm going to go through the major features. Up here in the neck,
these are the salivary glands and these little round things on top of them are the lymph nodes.
If you lift that up here in the neck area, this ringed structure is the trachea and the esophagus
is located next to it. You follow that down, get to the heart. You can see this rat has been injected,
this is the aorta and then you have the two crowded arteries that go up into the neck.
There's your heart and the two organs to each side are the lungs.
Here, between the thoracic cavity, just like the test cavity and the abdominal cavity,
we have this muscle, that's the diaphragm and the liver. The front lobe of the liver with this
little cleft in it is the median lobe. Then we have the left lateral lobe and then on this side is the
right lateral lobe. We lift the liver up, you'll notice there is no gallbladder. There's a gallbladder
in humans but not in rats and this pouch structure here is the stomach. You can see from this angle,
the esophagus enters the stomach right there. Then the stomach curves around and the first section
is the duodenum. Now while we're here, this thing that kind of looks like a finger that goes across
the stomach, that's the spleen. This bumpy yellowish stuff is what remains of the pancreas,
which is a gland and it doesn't preserve very well. Going back to the stomach, we're going to
follow the stomach down. This is the duodenum. Then when you get to this curly stuff, this is the
dejunum. If you stretch it out, you can see the mesentery and the mesentery arteries that are in
that dejunum. You follow that all the way down. It's very long in the rat. You get to this pouch.
This is the seacum. Humans have an appendix there and the small intestine, which is starts at the
duodenum, goes to the dejunum and then it's last little stretch here where it enters into the
seacum is the ilium. It goes DJ-ilium. Then as we follow the seacum up, it now becomes the large
intestine. The large intestine goes up, over and down. This is the asin dang colon. This is the transverse
colon and this is the de-sin dang colon that leads the heads out here at the rectum. These two little
tubes don't get those confused. Those are actually uterine horns and are part of the female reproductive
system. You can follow those up and get to the ovary. I think that about the bladder. Let's see.
This little nub right there is a urinary bladder and it connects to the kidneys here and sometimes
you can find the ureter, which is little tube that leads here from the kidney down to the bladder.
But it'd be kind of hard to find on some of these. Sometimes I can wiggle it. It's kind of up there.
It's very tiny. Kidney, your ureter, bladder.
